name: Aceruloplasminaemia
aliases: CP-related neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation

clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by biallelic CP variants that abolish the ferroxidase activity of caeruloplasmin, producing tissue iron overload and a form of neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation.
The classic adult-onset triad is retinal degeneration, diabetes mellitus and progressive neurological disease, typically emerging from mid-adulthood.
Neurological features are predominantly extrapyramidal — craniofacial dyskinesia (blepharospasm, grimacing), chorea, dystonia and parkinsonism — with ataxia, cognitive decline and psychiatric change.
A microcytic anaemia with low serum iron but raised ferritin is characteristic and, together with diabetes, often precedes neurological onset by years.
Serum caeruloplasmin is absent or very low and serum copper is low, yet the accumulating metal is iron, not copper — the reverse of what the copper studies might suggest.
Brain MRI shows striking iron-related hypointensity on T2 and susceptibility-weighted sequences in the basal ganglia, thalamus and dentate nucleus, with hepatic iron deposition.
It is one of the few identifiable neurodegeneration-with-brain-iron-accumulation disorders in which iron chelation and antioxidant strategies are considered.
Never give iron for the anaemia — supplemental iron worsens the underlying tissue iron overload.
reference.pathophysiology: Caeruloplasmin is a copper-dependent multicopper oxidase whose ferroxidase activity converts ferrous to ferric iron, a step required for iron export through ferroportin and its loading onto transferrin. Biallelic loss-of-function CP variants eliminate this ferroxidase function, so iron released from cells cannot be oxidised and mobilised, and it becomes trapped intracellularly in the tissues that rely on caeruloplasmin — particularly astrocytes in the brain, hepatocytes, pancreatic islet cells and the retina. Progressive intracellular iron accumulation catalyses free-radical generation and oxidative injury, causing neuronal loss in the basal ganglia and cerebellum, destruction of pancreatic islets with resulting diabetes, and retinal degeneration. Serum copper is low because most circulating copper is normally carried on caeruloplasmin, but systemic copper handling is otherwise intact — a key distinction from Wilson disease, in which caeruloplasmin is also low but the pathology is copper overload. The mismatch of a microcytic anaemia with low circulating iron yet raised ferritin reflects iron sequestration within tissues rather than true iron deficiency.
additionalDifferentials: Wilson disease — also shows low caeruloplasmin but reflects copper rather than iron overload, and is the principal mimic

additionalInvestigations: Serum caeruloplasmin (absent or markedly reduced) with serum copper (low)
Iron studies showing low serum iron, low transferrin saturation and markedly raised ferritin
Full blood count and film demonstrating microcytic anaemia
Fasting glucose and glycated haemoglobin to detect diabetes mellitus
Brain MRI with T2, T2* and susceptibility-weighted imaging for iron deposition; hepatic iron assessment by MRI
CP gene sequencing for molecular confirmation
Ophthalmological and retinal evaluation including optical coherence tomography, and urinary copper measurement to help distinguish Wilson disease
redFlags: A new movement disorder or cognitive decline arising in a patient with diabetes and anaemia
Rapidly progressive extrapyramidal signs or craniofacial dyskinesia
Progressive visual loss from retinal degeneration
Emerging psychiatric disturbance with neurological signs in mid-adulthood
reference.prognosis: The condition is progressively neurodegenerative; early iron chelation may slow systemic iron accumulation and possibly retard neurological progression, but established neurological deficits are often irreversible and disability accrues over years.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing Wilson disease because caeruloplasmin is low in both, and consequently pursuing inappropriate copper-directed treatment
Attributing the anaemia to simple iron deficiency and prescribing iron, which aggravates tissue iron overload
Failing to anticipate that iron chelation can worsen the anaemia and requires careful monitoring
Overlooking early isolated diabetes or anaemia as heralds of the disorder years before neurological onset
Not recognising the low serum copper as a secondary consequence of absent caeruloplasmin rather than a primary copper disorder
references: Inborn errors of metabolism reference texts (standard reference)
Disorders of metal metabolism clinical references (standard reference)
management: Iron chelation with an agent such as deferasirox, deferoxamine or deferiprone as the disease-specific mainstay to lower tissue iron and retard progression
Monitor haemoglobin closely during chelation because the underlying microcytic anaemia may worsen, adjusting therapy or adding erythropoietin as required
Antioxidant supplementation such as vitamin E to limit iron-mediated oxidative injury
Manage the diabetes mellitus with standard antidiabetic therapy including insulin
Symptomatic control of the extrapyramidal movement disorder with support for cognitive decline and ataxia through neurology, alongside retinal monitoring
Regular surveillance of iron studies and ferritin, glycaemic status and neurological and ophthalmological function
Genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder to enable early treatment of affected relatives
